title: Energy, population and disease
summary: Everyday civilization depends on energy. Food sustains bodies, animals provide traction, and fuels support heating and production. The energy a society can obtain, convert and mobilize affects the population, labor and infrastructure it can maintain. Energy alone, however, does not organize society.

blocks.text: Everyday civilization depends on energy. Food sustains bodies, animals provide traction, and fuels support heating and production. The energy a society can obtain, convert and mobilize affects the population, labor and infrastructure it can maintain. Energy alone, however, does not organize society.

Population also means more than a total. Density, age structure, migration and arrangements for work change resource demands and forms of cooperation. More people can enable greater specialization while placing heavier pressure on land, food and public infrastructure. Numbers acquire meaning within a particular structure.

Disease introduces another condition often overlooked in historical accounts. Concentrated populations, long-distance movement and exchange networks can create new opportunities for pathogens. Connections carry not only goods and knowledge but also risks that societies may be poorly equipped to manage.

These conditions interact. Changes in energy can transform production and cities; population changes reorganize labor and resources; disease can interrupt established arrangements. Capabilities and vulnerabilities therefore need to be considered together. More resources, more people or wider networks are not independent proofs of progress.
